clue.text: Local punching setter in narrow alleyway

indicators.note: a punch drives straight through whatever it lands on, so one piece is forced into the middle of the other

parts.note: gel is what sets hair, so the setter here is the tube on the bathroom shelf
your local is the pub down the road, and a pub is an inn

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is almost always the person who wrote the clue, which is exactly why it is worth doubting here — this one sets hair.
explanation.definitionFit: narrow alleyway -> GINNEL: the northern English word for the passage squeezed between two buildings, everyday speech in Yorkshire and Lancashire.

clue.text: Epic tale of single boy going round India

parts.note: a single is one, and one is I in Roman numerals

indicators.note: what goes round something ends up wrapped on either side of it, so the letter named next is enclosed

parts.note: a boy is a lad, and it opens up after its first letter
India is I in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: Two different I's from two different conventions, a Roman numeral and a radio call sign, which is how the clue gets away with using one twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Epic tale -> ILIAD: Homer's poem on the siege of Troy is the founding example of the epic, so the definition names it by its genre.

clue.text: D'Artagnan finally brought up "All for one, and one…" — a bloomer

indicators.note: it asks for the last letter of the name beside it and nothing else
in a down entry, what is brought up is read from the bottom square towards the top, so those letters arrive in the opposite order

parts.note: the last letter of the fourth musketeer's name
three letters lifted straight out of the motto
'for one' is how a clue says e.g., the abbreviation of 'for example'
one is I again, and ALL, EG and I then climb back up the entry together

explanation.walkthrough: The musketeers' motto is quoted for the surface and then read as three unrelated scraps of crosswordese, so the quotation marks help you not at all.
explanation.definitionFit: a bloomer -> NIGELLA: love-in-a-mist is a garden flower and so a thing that blooms; the loaf and the blunder are the senses being dangled.

clue.text: Survives very boring falsehoods

indicators.note: to bore is to drill a hole through the middle of something, so that letter goes inside

parts.note: falsehoods are lies, and the word splits after its second letter
V is the standard abbreviation for very

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and the middle one is an instruction rather than an opinion — 'boring' is not describing the falsehoods at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Survives -> LIVES: to live through a crash is to survive it, the same third-person verb, and 'he lives!' makes exactly that claim.

clue.text: Notes OAP is terrible stirrer

indicators.note: a terrible version of something has come out wrong, and letters that came out wrong are no longer in the order they were given

parts.note: five letters taken as letters, not as music or as money
an old age pensioner joins the mix, initials and all

explanation.walkthrough: The surface accuses a pensioner of stirring up trouble, and the answer is what stirs your tea — a different sort of stirrer entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: stirrer -> TEASPOON: the spoon you stir a cup with, so the definition names it by the job it does rather than by its size.

clue.text: Oscar then interrupts wild driving manoeuvres

indicators.note: wild means untamed and out of hand, so nothing it points at stays in the order it arrived in

parts.note: Oscar is O in the phonetic alphabet
fourteen letters at face value, which with the O makes the fifteen the grid wants

explanation.walkthrough: 'Interrupts' reads as an instruction to push one piece into another, and that is the trap: here it is fourteen letters of raw fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: driving manoeuvres -> THREE-POINT TURNS: the turn-in-the-road every learner is tested on, named for the three moves it takes.

clue.text: Save a piece for eccentric male

indicators.note: an eccentric sits off-centre, out of the usual arrangement, and so do these letters

parts.note: a piece of something is a part of it, and the 'a' comes along too
the three letters of 'for' knocked out of their usual order
M is the standard abbreviation for male

explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' at the front looks like a verb about rescuing or economising, and it is really the preposition of 'all save one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Save -> APART FROM: both introduce the exception to a statement, so 'all save one' and 'all apart from one' say the same thing.

clue.text: Exercises with group running in pack

parts.note: PE is physical education, the school lesson where you exercise
a lot is a group of things taken together
a play or a film that is running is on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Running in' looks like one phrase about a race and is really two jobs: 'running' is its own piece and 'in' only joins the halves of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: pack -> PELOTON: the main bunch in a road race, from the French for platoon, and commentators call that group the pack.

clue.text: Old tin cans ultimately pollute large body of water

indicators.note: to can something is to seal it inside a tin, so what follows goes in the middle

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: the ultimate letter of a word is its last one, and that is all this takes

parts.note: a tin is a can, and it opens after its first letter
the last letter of pollute

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cans' is doing a verb's work in a sentence full of nouns — read it as 'puts in a tin' and the clue comes apart at once.
explanation.definitionFit: large body of water -> OCEAN: the biggest of them all, the continuous salt water covering most of the planet, so 'large' does the sorting.

clue.text: Heather is untruthful, taking year out

indicators.note: taking here means taking away — the piece named is subtracted from the word rather than added to it

parts.note: somebody untruthful is lying
Y is the standard abbreviation for year, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' reads as a woman's name in a sentence about honesty, and it is the plant — the heather that covers a British moor.
explanation.definitionFit: Heather -> LING: ling is the common heather of moorland, Calluna vulgaris, so the definition is the ordinary name for the same plant.

clue.text: Seller with Visa unusual in palace location

indicators.note: what is unusual departs from the normal arrangement, and these letters have departed from theirs

parts.note: six letters taken at face value, not as a person
four more letters, capital V and all

explanation.walkthrough: A trader taking cards is a plausible little scene, which is what fodder wants to look like: two ordinary nouns and nothing to see.
explanation.definitionFit: palace location -> VERSAILLES: the town outside Paris where Louis XIV built his palace, so the answer names the place rather than the building.

clue.text: When housing benefit gets bit of money for youth

indicators.note: housing something is giving it a roof over its head, so it ends up inside

parts.note: as means when — 'as I left' is 'when I left' — and it opens after its first letter
the dole is unemployment benefit
a cent is the small change of a dollar or a euro

explanation.walkthrough: The benefits-office surface is built entirely out of the wordplay's own words, so nothing in it is pointing at a person of that age.
explanation.definitionFit: youth -> ADOLESCENT: a youth is a person in their teens, which is precisely the stage the answer names; both are nouns for the same years.

clue.text: Quietly happy to leave rip-off shelter

indicators.note: what leaves a word has walked out of it, so those letters are not in the answer

parts.note: content is happy in a settled, undemonstrative way
a con is a swindle, and it is the three letters that walk

explanation.walkthrough: 'Quietly' looks like the usual signal for P, the musician's piano, and here it is simply half of a two-word definition.
explanation.definitionFit: shelter -> TENT: canvas over poles is the shelter you carry with you, so the definition names it by what it is for.

clue.text: Perhaps Robbie cut cakes as prepared in opulent mansion

indicators.note: a name that has been cut comes up a letter short, and it is the tail that goes
to cake something is to coat it all over, so the outer word closes right round the inner one

parts.note: Margot Robbie is one Robbie among many, which is what 'perhaps' is warning you about
a la is the menu French for done in the style of, as in a la carte

explanation.walkthrough: Everything reads as a tea party: 'cut cakes' is a knife and a plate on the surface, and two separate instructions underneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: opulent mansion -> MAR-A-LAGO: the gilded Palm Beach estate, so the definition names it by the kind of house it is rather than by its owner.

clue.text: Past master's second attempt

indicators.note: it counts along the word beside it and keeps only the letter standing in position two

parts.note: the second letter of master, which is also the A of an MA
an attempt at something is simply GO, the word behind 'give it your best shot'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Past master' is a set phrase for an expert, and reading those two words together is what stops the clue splitting where it should.
explanation.definitionFit: Past -> AGO: both put an event behind us, so 'two years ago' and 'the past two years' point at the same stretch of time.

clue.text: European ignored by pescetarian probing suitable candidate

indicators.note: what is ignored is left out, so that letter never makes it into the word beside it

parts.note: apt means suitable, and it parts after its second letter

indicators.note: a probe goes in to have a look round, so this piece pushes into the middle of the other

parts.note: a pelican lives on the fish it scoops up, so it keeps to a pescetarian's diet
E is the standard abbreviation for European, and it is the letter the bird loses

explanation.walkthrough: The bird is the joke: 'pescetarian' describes a diet, and only one creature anywhere in the clue actually keeps to it.
explanation.definitionFit: candidate -> APPLICANT: someone who has put in for a job is a candidate for it, though the answer insists on the application itself.

clue.text: Shy singer picked up in French city

indicators.note: you pick up a sound rather than a spelling, so what counts is what the words are heard as

parts.note: a wren is the small skulking songbird of the hedgerow, its W is silent, and French drops the ending of the city's name the same way

explanation.walkthrough: French keeps the -nes on the page and swallows it in the mouth, which is how six letters can sound like three.
explanation.definitionFit: French city -> RENNES: the capital of Brittany, a real city in the north-west, so the definition places it by country.

clue.text: Stop loan, wasting pound

indicators.note: what is wasted is thrown away, so the letter named next is gone from the word

parts.note: to loan something is to lend it
L is the pound's letter, from the Latin libra, as on the £ sign

explanation.walkthrough: Money and lending sit together so naturally that 'pound' reads as part of the loan rather than as one letter to be thrown out.
explanation.definitionFit: Stop -> END: to end a meeting is to stop it, the same transitive verb; the finishing-point noun is the word's other half.

clue.text: Leave, then go back and chat

parts.note: to leave is to go

indicators.note: an across entry runs right to left when it comes back, so the word beside it is written in reverse

parts.note: 'go' the second time is the lavatory euphemism, piss, and that is the word turned round

explanation.walkthrough: The same little verb is clued twice in two different senses, which is why 'go' can sit in the answer and in the wordplay without repeating itself.
explanation.definitionFit: chat -> GOSSIP: idle talk about other people's business, so 'chat' catches the informality while the answer adds who is being talked about.

clue.text: Dictator getting a Parisian to replace American in hot spot

indicators.note: the new piece does not join the word, it stands exactly where the old one was and the old one goes

parts.note: a satrap was a Persian provincial governor, long a byword for a petty tyrant
'a' in Paris is un
A is the standard abbreviation for American, and it is the letter that makes way

explanation.walkthrough: Satrap is worth banking: it turns up whenever a setter wants a dictator and the letters S, A, T, R, P.
explanation.definitionFit: hot spot -> SUNTRAP: a sheltered corner that catches and holds the sun, so it is warm by design rather than dangerous.

clue.text: New poem about repellent domesticated worm

indicators.note: a thing placed about another goes round it, closing on both sides
to repel is to drive back, and the word it points at is driven back the way it came

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
an ode is a poem, and with the N in front it makes the shell
a domesticated animal is tame, and this is the word that gets driven back

explanation.walkthrough: 'Repellent domesticated worm' reads as one phrase about an unpleasant creature, and the two adjectives belong to quite different jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: worm -> NEMATODE: the roundworms of soil and gut, so 'worm' is the plain-English name for the whole group of them.

clue.text: Left alone dangerous bears with hooked claws

indicators.note: to bear something is to carry it, so the words in front are carrying the answer along inside them

parts.note: the end of 'left', all of 'alone' and the start of 'dangerous' run straight into one another

explanation.walkthrough: Three ordinary words in a row about wildlife, and the answer is lying across the joins between them without the surface twitching once.
explanation.definitionFit: with hooked claws -> TALONED: talons are the curved claws of a bird of prey, so the answer is the adjective for having a set.

clue.text: Steal ring from East Scotland town

indicators.note: in an across entry anything coming from the east is travelling right to left, so it is written backwards

parts.note: to nab something is to steal it
a ring is a circle, drawn as the letter O

explanation.walkthrough: 'East Scotland' looks like one place and is two jobs — the east belongs to the wordplay, and the town it hides is on the west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland town -> OBAN: the ferry port in Argyll, gateway to the isles, so the definition simply places a real town in its country.

clue.text: British eggs on the up? Excellent!

parts.note: BR is the short form of British, familiar from British Rail

indicators.note: in a down entry, letters on the up are read from the bottom square towards the top

parts.note: ova are eggs in the biologist's Latin, and they are what climbs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Eggs on' reads as a single phrase meaning urges on, which is exactly the wrong place to break the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Excellent! -> BRAVO: the Italian shout an audience gives a singer, borrowed into English as the standard cry of approval.

clue.text: Hear client somehow not under suspicion

indicators.note: it admits the letters got where they are by no particular route, which is another way of saying they moved

parts.note: ten letters at face value, a lawyer and a verb dissolved into fodder

explanation.walkthrough: A solicitor listening to a client is a scene the wordplay borrows whole, and the definition is everything left in the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: not under suspicion -> IN THE CLEAR: the idiom for having been cleared of blame, said of the person the police have finished with.

clue.text: Church official's European articles

parts.note: el is the Spanish for 'the'
der is the German for 'the', and two of Europe's articles are all the clue needs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' is plural for a reason: the clue wants two of them, from two languages, and neither one is the English 'a' or 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Church official -> ELDER: in Presbyterian and other reformed churches an elder is the lay officer who helps govern the congregation.

clue.text: Fuss over nasty smell in Filipino dish

indicators.note: in a down entry, whatever sits over something else is written above it, so this piece comes first

parts.note: much ado about nothing — ado is fuss
BO is body odour

explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are staples worth banking: 'ado' for fuss and BO for a smell turn up several times a week between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Filipino dish -> ADOBO: the national dish of the Philippines, meat stewed in vinegar, soy and garlic, a name English borrowed whole.

clue.text: Maybe blonde female character ran to the audience

parts.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female
the air of a person or a place is its character — an air of menace, an air of calm

indicators.note: an audience hears words and never sees them, so the spelling is free to change on the way

parts.note: to hare off somewhere is to run flat out, and 'hared' said aloud is written the other way

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the soundalike is the hair itself: a running hare and a head of hair make exactly the same noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Maybe blonde -> FAIR-HAIRED: blonde is one shade of fair hair, so 'maybe' marks the definition as an example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Great English scientist, losing heart, produces gas

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, and losing it takes the central letters out

parts.note: Isaac Newton is the great English scientist, and the W and T at his centre are what go

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is one small word at the end of a sentence about physics, which is where a setter puts it when the surface is doing all the shouting.
explanation.definitionFit: gas -> NEON: one of the noble gases, the one that glows orange in a discharge tube, so the definition names the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Desserts in school regularly loathed by son

parts.note: a comp is a comprehensive school

indicators.note: it takes letters at a regular step, every second one, instead of the whole word

parts.note: every second letter of lOaThEd
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.walkthrough: A miserable school dinner is the picture, and the three pieces come from three registers: slang, a letter trick and an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Desserts -> COMPOTES: a compote is fruit stewed in syrup and served at the end of a meal, so the plural names a kind of pudding.

clue.text: Common UK mammal given baguettes possibly to eat, according to Spooner

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner traded the opening sounds of two words, so his version of a phrase arrives with its heads swapped

parts.note: to be given something to eat is to be fed
a baguette is a long rectangular cut of gemstone, and rocks is the trade's slang for stones
trade the F and the R at the front of the two words and the sound that comes out is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Baguettes look like lunch and are jewellery here, so the surface's whole job is to keep you standing in the bakery.
explanation.definitionFit: Common UK mammal -> RED FOX: Britain's most widespread wild carnivore, at home in city and country, and 'red' names the species rather than a colour.
